why: The set is a multiset that gains and loses arbitrary values, and after every query you need its current minimum and maximum. That is two priority queues (a min-heap and a max-heap) over the same values, with lazy deletion because a heap cannot remove an arbitrary element.
hints: After each query you only need two numbers: the smallest and the largest value still present. Which structure gives you an extreme in O(log n)?
Keep a min-heap and a max-heap of every pushed value, plus a count map of how many copies are really alive. A pop just decrements the count; the stale copy stays in the heaps for now.
Before reading a heap's top, pop entries whose live count is 0 (lazy deletion). Each value is pushed and popped at most once per heap, so the total is O(n log n).
pitfalls: Values can repeat: popping one copy of 5 must leave the other copies alive, so count copies instead of using a plain set.
Products reach 10^18; fine in Python but needs a 64-bit type elsewhere.
Clean both heaps lazily: a popped value may still sit at the top of either one.
statement:
Start with an empty multiset elements (values may repeat). You are given two arrays of length n: operations and x. Query i is:

  • push x[i]: insert one copy of x[i] into elements.
  • pop x[i]: remove one copy of x[i] from elements (it is guaranteed to be there).

After each query, record min(elements) × max(elements). Return the n recorded products in order.

Worked example. operations = [push, push, push, pop], x = [1, 2, 3, 1]:

  1. push 1 → {1}: min 1, max 1, product 1.
  2. push 2 → {1, 2}: min 1, max 2, product 2.
  3. push 3 → {1, 2, 3}: min 1, max 3, product 3.
  4. pop 1 → {2, 3}: min 2, max 3, product 6.

Answer: [1, 2, 3, 6].
